title: Siddu
subtitle: Fermented steamed wheat bread

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and Regional Details
Name of the Food:Siddu — a traditional fermented, steamed wheat bread.
Region/Community: Siddu is associated with the hill regions of
Himachal Pradesh, particularly Kullu and
Shimla.
Context:Siddu is a traditional home-cooked food prepared using wheat
dough and a savoury filling. It is commonly served hot with ghee,
chutney, or dal. Fermentation and steaming distinguish it from
ordinary flatbreads.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin Story:
Siddu developed as part of the traditional food culture of
Himachal Pradesh's mountain communities. Research documents
it as a fermented, steam-cooked bread. However, a single
confirmed inventor or exact origin date is not established by the
sources cited here.
Cultural Meaning:
Siddu represents the use of locally available wheat and traditional
fermentation and steaming techniques. Preparing the dough and
allowing it to ferment requires knowledge passed between cooks
and generations.

Story/Folklore:
No reliably documented folk tale about Siddu's origin was
identified in the sources used here. Its traditional preparation
can be presented as an example of Himachali food knowledge.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main Ingredients and Preparation Method
Ingredients:
Wheat flour, Water, Yeast, Ground lentils,walnuts or poppy seeds
for the filling, Salt, Ghee or chutney for serving.
Preparation Method:

First, wheat flour is mixed with water to prepare a soft dough.
The dough is allowed to rest, and a filling made from lentils,
walnuts or poppy seeds may be added. The dough is shaped
into bread and steamed until it is fully cooked. Siddu is usually
served hot with ghee or chutney.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4) Why it is considered forgotten or at risk:
Time-Consuming Process:
Preparing the dough and steaming the bread takes time.
Shift to Commercial Fast Food:
Some people may prefer quicker foods and steaming the
Siddu requires patience.

Decline in traditional knowledge:
Family cooking methods may not always be recorded.
People may prefer ready-made flour from shops.

1) Title and Regional Details:
Name of the Food:
Chainsoo — a traditional dish made from roasted black gram
(urad dal).
Region/Community:
Chainsoo is a traditional dish from Uttarakhand, particularly
associated with Garhwali cuisine.
Context:
Chainsoo is a thick lentil dish usually eaten with rice or roti. Its
distinctive flavour comes from roasting the black gram before
grinding and cooking it.
sections.history:
2) History and Cultural Importance:
Origin Story:
Chainsoo is a traditional food of Uttarakhand, especially the
Garhwal region. It is made using black gram, also called urad
dal. It developed as part of the local mountain food tradition.
Its exact origin date is not known.
Cultural Meaning:
The dish reflects traditional Pahari cooking, in which locally
available pulses and spices are used to prepare filling everyday
meals. Roasting the lentils before cooking gives Chainsoo its
characteristic flavour and texture.

Story/Folklore:
No verified folk tale specifically explaining the origin of Chainsoo
was found in the cited sources. Its traditional preparation and its
connection with Garhwali cuisine provide a documented cultural
story without adding unsupported legends.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main Ingredients and Preparation Method:
Ingredients:
Black gram, Water, salt, Cumin, Coriander powder, Turmeric,
Oil or ghee, Optional ginger, garlic and chilli.

Preparation Method:
Clean the black gram and roast it in a pan.
Allow it to cool and grind it coarsely.
Heat oil or ghee and add the spices.
Add the ground lentils.
Pour in water.
Cook until thick and soft and then serve with rice.

Younger generations may become less familiar with Chainsoo.

Slow cooking is needed to get the traditional taste.

title: Haak
subtitle: Kashmiri leafy-green preparation

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and Regional Details:
Name of the Food:Haak or Haakh — a traditional Kashmiri leafy-green
dish.
Region/Community:
Haak is associated with Kashmir, particularly Kashmiri household
food traditions. It is prepared in different homes using locally
available leafy greens.
Context:Haak is generally prepared by cooking leafy greens in water with
ingredients such as mustard oil, salt, and sometimes garlic or
chillies. It is commonly eaten with rice and is valued as a
familiar everyday food.
sections.history:
2) History and Cultural Importance:
Origin Story:
Cultural Meaning: Haak represents the relationship between Kashmiri
food culture, seasonal vegetables, and household
cooking. It is more than a special-occasion dish: it
has a place in ordinary meals and family food
traditions.
Story/Folklore:
A single verified folk tale explaining the origin of Haak was
not identified in the cited research.
Haak is a traditional leafy-green dish from Kashmir. It has been
prepared in Kashmiri homes for generations. People use
locally available green vegetables to make this dish. Its exact
origin date is not known.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main Ingredients and Preparation Method:
Ingredients:
Haak leaves, Water, Salt, Mustard oil, Green chilli or other
seasonings.
Preparation Method:
The leaves are washed thoroughly to remove dirt. A little oil
is heated in a pot, and the seasonings are added. The greens
and water are then added and cooked until the leaves
become tender. The salt is adjusted, and Haak is served hot,
commonly with rice.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4) Why it is considered forgotten or at risk:
Time-Consuming Process:
Fresh leafy greens must be cleaned and sorted.
Traditional cooking requires attention to the greens and their texture.
Preparing fresh vegetables may be less convenient than using ready-
made meals.
Shift to Commercial Fast Food:
Packaged foods and restaurant meals may replace home-cooked
vegetable dishes on busy days.
Decline in Traditional Milling:
Family cooking methods may not always be recorded.

title: Ker Sangri
subtitle: Desert berries and khejri pods

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and Regional Details:
Name of the Food: Ker Sangri — a traditional Rajasthani dish made from
desert berries and pods.
Region/Community:
Ker Sangri is a traditional dish from Rajasthan. It developed in the dry
desert regions of the state. People used desert berries and pods that
could grow in difficult weather conditions.It is also served at Marwari
weddings and other special occasions.
Context: Ker Sangri shows how people in Rajasthan used available desert
plants to prepare food. Drying the ingredients helped them store
food for later use. This reflects the traditional knowledge of
desert communities.
sections.history:
2) History and Cultural Importance:
Origin Story:
Cultural Meaning:
Ker Sangri reflects local knowledge of desert plants and how to
prepare food in a dry climate. It is recognised by Rajasthan
Tourism as an authentic regional preparation and is associated
with Marwari wedding celebrations.
Story/Folklore:
Ker Sangri is a traditional dish from Rajasthan. It developed in the
dry desert regions of the state. People used desert berries and
pods that could grow in difficult weather conditions.It is also
served at Marwari weddings and other special occasions.

No specific, verified folk tale about the origin of Ker Sangri was identified in the
sources used here. Its documented cultural story is its relationship with
Rajasthan's desert environment and the traditional use of locally available plants.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main Ingredients and Preparation Method:
Ingredients: Ker berries, Sangri pods, Water for soaking, Oil or ghee,
Cumin and other spices, Chilli powder, Salt,
Dry mango powder(optional)
Preparation Method:
The dried ker berries and sangri pods are washed and soaked as needed.
They are cooked until tender, and excess water is drained. Oil or ghee is
heated with spices, and the ingredients are added. Everything is mixed
and cooked until the spices coat the berries and pods. The dish is often
served with roti.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4) Why it is considered forgotten or at risk:
Time-Consuming Process:
Dried ingredients may need cleaning, soaking, and careful cooking.
Removing impurities and preparing the ingredients takes time.
Shift to Commercial Fast Food:
Ready-made meals can be more convenient for busy households.
Restaurant and packaged versions may not preserve every
household's traditional method.
Decline in Traditional Milling:
Milling is not a major part of preparing Ker Sangri, so this factor is
not directly applicable.

title: Mah di Dal
subtitle: Punjabi black gram dal

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and Regional Details:
Name of the Food:Mah di Dal — a Punjabi lentil dish made from black
gram, also known as urad dal.
Region/Community:
Mah di Dal is associated with Punjab and Punjabi food traditions.
Household recipes differ in their use of whole or split black gram
and in their seasonings.
Context:
Mah di Dal is a filling pulse-based dish that can be eaten with roti
or rice. It represents the importance of pulses in Punjabi cooking
alongside wheat breads, vegetables, and dairy products.
sections.history:
2) History and Cultural Importance:
Origin Story:
Mah di Dal developed within the broader tradition of cooking pulses
in Punjabi households. Black gram is used in many Indian regional
cuisines, and the exact origin date of this particular Punjabi
preparation is not established by the sources cited here.
Cultural Meaning: The dish reflects the importance of home-cooked meals
and pulse-based foods in Punjabi cuisine. Its ingredients
are relatively simple, and the recipe can be adapted to
family preferences.
Story/Folklore:
No specific, verified folk tale about the origin of Mah di Dal was identified
in the sources used here. Its cultural significance is better supported by
its place in Punjabi household cooking than by an unverified origin legend.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main Ingredients and Preparation Method:
Ingredients: Black gram, Onion, Ginger and garlic, Tomatoes, Cumin
and other spices, Salt, Oil or ghee
Preparation Method:
The black gram is washed and, when necessary, soaked
before cooking. It is soaked until it becomes soft. Ginger,
garlic, spices, and optional onion and tomato are cooked
separately and mixed into the dal. The mixture is simmered
until it becomes thick and flavourful, then served with roti
or rice.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4) Why it is considered forgotten or at risk:
Time-Consuming Process:
Whole black gram may require soaking and extended cooking.
Quick meals may be preferred when people have limited time.
Shift to Commercial Fast Food:
Ready-made meals and restaurant food may replace home
cooking on some days.
Commercial versions may differ from traditional family
recipes
Decline in Traditional Milling:
Milling is not a central step in preparing Mah di Dal, so this
factor is not directly applicable.

title: Hawaijar
subtitle: Fermented soybean

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and regional background
Name of the food:Hawaijar
Region/community: Manipur, Northeast India; particularly associated with
the Meitei food tradition.
Context:
Hawaijar is a traditional fermented soybean food with a sticky texture,
alkaline character, and strong aroma. It is eaten as a condiment or side dish
and is also used in dishes such as chagem pomba, which combines rice,
vegetables, and other ingredients.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin story:
The exact date and inventor of Hawaijar have not been established.
Researchers explain that soybean cultivation and fermentation became
part of the region's food culture over a long period. The 2023 review by
Thangjam Anand Singh and co-authors discusses both local traditions and
possible historical routes by which soybeans reached the region. These
should not be presented as a proven single origin story.
Cultural meaning:
Provides a plant-based protein source in traditional diets.
Functions as a flavouring ingredient and accompaniment to rice.
Traditional household production has been an important source of
local knowledge and income, especially for women.

Story or folklore:
No verified folk tale specifically explaining the invention of Hawaijar was
identified in the cited research. For your book, interview a traditional
producer or community elder and, with permission, include their
account rather than inventing a legend.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main ingredients and preparation method
Main base: Soybeans
Other ingredients:
Hawaijar itself is made primarily from soybeans. When served, it may be
combined with onion, salt, and chilli, including the local king chilli known as
umorok.

Preparation technique:
Clean and soak soybeans.
Boil them until soft.
Drain and cool the beans.
Place them in a suitable traditional fermentation container.
Allow fermentation to develop the characteristic sticky texture,
aroma, and alkaline properties.
Eat it as a condiment or incorporate it into dishes.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4) Why it may be at risk
Time-consuming process:
Preparation requires soaking, cooking, fermentation, and knowledge of
suitable conditions.

Shift to commercial fast food:
Convenient alternatives may compete with traditional foods, but the cited
research does not establish that fast food has caused a measured decline
in Hawaijar consumption.
Decline in traditional knowledge:
The review describes production as a household skill passed between
generations. This makes documentation and transmission of knowledge
important, although it does not prove that the practice is disappearing.

title: Soibum
subtitle: Fermented bamboo shoots

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and regional background
Name of the food: Soibum.
Region/community: Manipur, Northeast India; prepared by communities
including the Meitei and Meitei-Pangal.
Context:Soibum is a sour, fermented bamboo-shoot product used in curries,
vegetable dishes, and other local preparations. It is also sold in local
markets, so it is better described as a regional heritage food than as an
extinct dish.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin story: The precise date and individual responsible for inventing
Soibum are unknown. Its development is associated with
communities using locally available bamboo shoots and
fermentation to preserve a seasonal ingredient for later use.
Cultural meaning:
Connects local biodiversity with everyday cooking.
Preserves bamboo shoots beyond their short fresh season.
Forms part of the region's distinctive sour and savoury food traditions.

The academic literature documents traditional production methods but
does not establish a specific founding legend for Soibum. A community
interview could supply an oral history, provided it is attributed to the
storyteller and not presented as universally accepted fact.
Story or folklore:
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main ingredients and preparation method:
Main ingredient: Tender bamboo shoots, from locally used species.
Other ingredients:
Water may be involved in washing and processing. Some methods use
leaves or lined fermentation chambers to hold the shoots. Salt is not
necessarily the defining ingredient in every traditional method.

Preparation technique:
Remove the tough outer sheaths from young bamboo shoots.
Wash and slice the tender inner portions.
Pack the slices tightly into a suitable fermentation vessel or traditional
chamber.
Allow fermentation to proceed under the chosen local method. Some
traditional methods take approximately 3–12 months.
Use the finished product in curries, pickles, and vegetable preparations.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4) Why it may be at risk:
Time-consuming process:
Some traditional methods require months of fermentation and dedicated
storage space.
Shift to commercial fast food:
Ready-to-eat foods may compete for convenience, but the available sources
do not prove that fast food has caused Soibum to decline.

title: Sinki
subtitle: Fermented radish taproot

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and regional background:
Name of the food: Sinki
Region/community:Himalayan communities, including those in Sikkim and
the Darjeeling hills.
Context:
Sinki is a fermented radish-root product that can be stored and later used in
soups and pickles. It represents a traditional method of preserving vegetables
in areas where fresh produce may be scarce seasonally.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin story:
The exact inventor and date of origin have not been established. A study by
Jyoti Prakash Tamang and co-authors on Himalayan fermented foods notes
oral histories concerning the accidental discovery of Gundruk and Sinki in
Nepal. One account relates to villagers fleeing conflict and leaving vegetables
behind. This is an oral-history explanation, not a verified historical event.
Cultural meaning:
Demonstrates knowledge of seasonal vegetable preservation.
Helps extend the use of radish beyond its fresh availability.
Reflects regional fermentation techniques and local food preferences.

Story or folklore:
The account about vegetables being left behind during periods of conflict is
recorded as oral history. If you use it, label it clearly as a community-origin
account rather than a proven fact.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main ingredients and preparation method:
Main ingredient: Radish roots.
Other ingredients:
The traditional process primarily relies on radish and fermentation; water
and suitable fermentation vessels are used during processing.

Preparation technique:
Wash the radish roots.
Cut or shred them and prepare them for fermentation.
Pack the material tightly into a traditional pit or vessel.
Allow natural fermentation to develop.
Remove the fermented product and dry it when required for longer storage.
Rehydrate and use in soup or pickle preparations.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4) Why it may be at risk
Time-consuming process:
Preparation involves processing the roots and allowing time for fermentation
and drying.

Shift to commercial fast food:

title: Gundruk
subtitle: Fermented leafy greens

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and regional background
Name of the food: Gundruk.
Region/community:
Himalayan communities, particularly in Nepal and the Darjeeling
hills and Sikkim in India.
Context: Gundruk is a fermented and dried leafy-vegetable product. It is used
in soups, curries, and pickles and helps preserve vegetables for
periods when fresh greens are less readily available.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin story:
Gundruk has a long regional tradition, but its exact origin date is not
established. Researchers have recorded oral accounts suggesting that it
may have developed accidentally when vegetables were left behind during
periods of conflict and later found to have fermented and dried. This
should be presented as an oral tradition rather than a proven historical
fact.
Cultural meaning:
Represents the traditional use of seasonal vegetables.
Shows how fermentation and drying reduce dependence on immediate
fresh-food availability.
Reflects regional knowledge passed between generations.

Story or folklore:
The oral account linking Gundruk's discovery to villagers fleeing conflict is
discussed in research on Himalayan fermented-food traditions. Include it as a
recorded origin account, and consider adding an interview with a local cook to
capture how the food is understood today.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main ingredients and preparation method:
Main ingredients:
Mustard leaves, radish leaves, cauliflower leaves, cabbage, or other suitable
local greens.

The traditional fermentation process primarily uses the vegetables
themselves; water may be used for cleaning. Salt is not necessarily required
in the traditional method described in the cited literature.
Other ingredients:
Preparation technique:
Collect and clean suitable leafy vegetables.
Wilt them for approximately one to two days, depending on conditions
and the recipe.
Crush them lightly and pack them tightly into a suitable container.
Cover the container and allow natural fermentation, commonly for
around 15–22 days in reported methods.
Remove the fermented greens and sun-dry them for storage.
Rehydrate or cook them as soup, curry, or pickle.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4) Why it may be at risk
Time-consuming process:
Preparation involves wilting, packing, fermentation, and drying, so it
takes considerably longer than simply cooking fresh vegetables
Shift to commercial fast food:
Convenience foods may compete with traditional home preparation, but
there is insufficient evidence in the cited studies to claim that fast food
alone is causing Gundruk's decline.

title: Pazhaya Sadham
subtitle: Overnight-soaked rice

sections.regionalDetails:

Name of the food:
Pazhaya Sadham, also called Pazhaya Soru in common usage.
Region/community:Tamil Nadu, South India.
Context: Pazhaya Sadham is a traditional rice preparation made by soaking
cooked rice in water, often overnight. Depending on the
preparation, natural fermentation can occur. It is commonly eaten
with accompaniments such as shallots, green chilli, curd, or other
local sides.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Cultural meaning:
Reflects the value of using cooked food rather than wasting it.
Connects rice-based diets with traditional household food practices.
Demonstrates how simple ingredients and overnight soaking can
produce a different flavour and texture.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:

Main ingredient: Cooked rice, traditionally including parboiled rice in the
research study.
Other ingredients: Water is used for soaking. Shallots, green chilli, curd, or
other accompaniments may be added when serving.

Cook the rice.
Allow it to cool.
Place it in a clean container and add water.
Leave it overnight using the traditional household
method.
The next day, eat it as soaked rice or as a naturally
fermented preparation, depending on the method
and conditions.
Serve with traditional accompaniments.
Preparation technique:
sections.whyAtRisk:

Time-consuming process:
It requires planning ahead and retaining rice for the next day's meal, rather
than preparing an immediate breakfast.
Shift to commercial fast food:

compete with traditional preparations. This is a plausible explanation for

measured decline in Pazhaya Sadham consumption.

title: Ragi Sangati
subtitle: Finger-millet staple

sections.regionalDetails:
Name of the food:
Region/community:
Context:
Rayalaseema, Andhra Pradesh, particularly rural
farming communities.
Ragi Sangati, also called Ragi Mudda.
A traditional staple made from finger-millet flour and water,
usually eaten with pappu, vegetable curry, chutney or spicy gravy.
It is associated with everyday meals rather than being exclusively a
festival dish. The Andhra Pradesh government documents it as a
regional food
1) Title and Regional Details
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin story:
Ragi became important in dry farming regions because finger millet
can grow under conditions where some other crops are difficult to
cultivate. Ragi Sangati developed as a practical way to turn the grain
into a filling staple. A precise origin date for the dish is not established
in the sources cited here.
Cultural meaning:
- Represents Rayalaseema's farming heritage.
- Reflects the use of locally grown millet in everyday cooking.
- Connects traditional food preparation with rural household life.

Story and folklore:
Ragi Sangati is part of the food memories of many Rayalaseema families,
particularly those who grew or processed their own millet. Family stories
about farming, grinding grain and eating sangati with homemade curry can
help document its cultural history. These are oral-history themes rather than
a single verified folk legend.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main ingredients and preparation method
Main mixture: Ragi flour and water.
Accompaniment: Pappu, vegetable curry, chutney or another regional gravy.

Cooking technique:
1. Bring water to a boil in a heavy pot.
2. Add some ragi flour and stir to prevent lumps.
3. Add the remaining flour gradually, stirring continuously.
4. Cook until the mixture becomes thick and cohesive.
5. Shape into balls while warm, using a suitable serving method.
6. Serve with curry or dal.

title: Ambali
subtitle: Fermented millet porridge

sections.regionalDetails:
Name of the food: Ambali, a traditional fermented millet porridge.
Region/community:
Telangana, particularly rural communities with a history of
millet consumption.
Context: Ambali is prepared using millet flour and water. Depending on local
tradition, the mixture may be cooked and allowed to ferment. It has
traditionally been consumed as a simple everyday food, especially
in warm weather.
1) Title and Regional Details
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance

MAHUA FLOWERS
The Forest's Seasonal Treasure
A. Name of the food: Mahua flowers.
Scientific name: Madhuca longifolia.
B. Region/community:
Central and eastern India, including parts of Madhya Pradesh,
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha and Maharashtra. Mahua is significant in
the food traditions of several Adivasi communities.
C. Context: Mahua flowers are collected when they fall from the tree during the
flowering season. They are used in traditional foods and preserved for later
consumption. Collection and processing also provide seasonal livelihood
opportunities for some forest-dependent households.
sections.history:
2. History and Cultural Importance
A. Origin story
The mahua tree has long been part of the forest landscapes and traditional resource systems of
central India. Communities have developed knowledge of its flowering season, collection
methods, drying and storage.
B. Cultural meaning
Mahua represents the relationship between forests, food, livelihood and community life. The
flowers can provide seasonal food and income, particularly for households that collect non-
timber forest products.
In some communities, mahua flowers are also associated with ceremonial beverages and social
gatherings. These uses vary between regions and communities.
C. Story and folklore
Mahua collection often involves people gathering flowers during the early morning when freshly
fallen flowers can be collected. The work requires knowledge of flowering periods, suitable
collection areas and drying practices.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3. Main Ingredients and Preparation Method
A. The dough or base
For a traditional mahua flatbread, dried or prepared mahua flowers can be combined
with a cereal flour such as wheat, jowar or another locally used grain.
B. The filling
Some recipes do not require a separate filling. Depending on local tradition, mahua
flowers may be combined with grain flour to prepare a sweet or mildly sweetened food.
C. The cooking technique
1.Collect mature flowers from a suitable, uncontaminated location.
2.Remove unwanted material and clean them appropriately.
3.Dry the flowers using a suitable method when they are intended for storage.
4.Rehydrate or prepare the flowers according to the recipe.
5.Combine them with flour or other traditional ingredients.
6.Cook the mixture as a flatbread, porridge or another locally documented dish.
Specific preparation methods should be verified with local cooks because recipes vary.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4. Why It Is Considered Forgotten or at Risk
A. Time-consuming processing
Collecting fallen flowers, removing impurities and drying them properly require
time and labour.
B. Shift to commercial fast food
Packaged sweets and commercially produced foods may replace some traditional
preparations, particularly where younger consumers have less familiarity with
mahua recipes.
C. Decline in traditional processing
Changes in forest access, markets, storage facilities and local livelihoods can affect
the continuation of traditional collection and processing practices.
Mahua remains economically and culturally important in many areas, so it is more
accurate to describe particular foods or preparation traditions as
underdocumented rather than claiming the entire food is disappearing.

4.The filling
Traditional flatbreads may be prepared without a filling. They can be served
with lentils, vegetables, chutneys or other regional accompaniments.
5.The cooking technique
Clean the grain and remove unwanted material.
Dry and mill it into flour.
Mix the flour with water to form a dough.
Shape the dough into a flatbread.
Cook it on a hot griddle until done.
sections.whyAtRisk:
4. Why It Is Considered Forgotten or at Risk
Time-consuming processing
Some traditional millet varieties require careful cleaning, dehusking and milling.
Preparing certain dishes by hand can also require considerable effort.
Shift to commercial fast food
Changing consumer preferences and the widespread availability of refined rice,
wheat products and packaged foods have reduced the use of some traditional millet dishes in particular communities.. Decline in traditional milling
Local processing knowledge, traditional milling facilities and the cultivation of local landraces may decline when demand falls.
The loss of a local variety can also mean losing recipes and agricultural knowledge associated with it.
However, millets are not universally forgotten. Interest in millet-based foods and their commercial availability has increased in

forested regions of Jharkhand, West Bengal, Meghalaya, Kerala,
Tamil Nadu and other parts of India.
C. Context: Wild mushrooms often appear during suitable seasonal
conditions, particularly during the monsoon in many regions.
Some communities gather and prepare locally recognised species
as vegetables or ingredients in traditional dishes.
Not every wild mushroom is edible. Correct species identification
is essential.
sections.history:

A. Origin story
Humans have collected wild fungi for food for a long time. In India, knowledge of locally
edible mushrooms has developed through observation, experience and the transmission
of practical knowledge between generations.

Wild mushrooms can contribute to seasonal dietary diversity and household livelihoods.
Their collection reflects knowledge of forest environments, rainfall, soil conditions and the
habitats in which particular species grow.
Research has documented edible mushrooms used by communities including the Khasi of
Meghalaya and the Kaani community of Tamil Nadu.

a vegetable, curry or ingredient in other dishes.
B. The filling
Mushrooms can be combined with locally used ingredients such as onions, spices and other
vegetables, depending on the regional recipe.

A general method for preparing verified edible mushrooms is:

B. Region/community: Forested and hilly regions of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra

communities maintain distinct knowledge of edible roots and tubers.
C. Context: Forest tubers are underground plant parts that can serve as
seasonal food resources. Different species vary in flavour, texture, nutritional
composition and preparation requirements.
Some tubers require specialised processing to reduce naturally occurring
irritants or toxic compounds. Species identification and correct preparation are
essential.
sections.history:

Roots and tubers have contributed to human diets in many parts of the world. In
India, some forest-dependent communities have traditionally gathered
particular species during suitable seasons, using knowledge of their habitats and
preparation requirements.
B. Cultural meaning
Forest tubers represent practical knowledge about the environment and
seasonal food availability. They may supplement cultivated grains and
vegetables, particularly in communities with access to diverse forest resources.
C. Story and folklore
The knowledge of tuber collection may include recognising vines and leaves,
identifying suitable harvesting periods and knowing which underground parts require
extensive processing.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:

A. Name of the food: Indigenous leafy greens, including locally
recognised amaranth varieties and other edible leaves.
B. Region/community: Indigenous and rural communities across
Jharkhand, Meghalaya, Kerala, West Bengal, Maharashtra and
other Indian states.
C. Context: Indigenous greens include cultivated and wild or semi-
wild leafy vegetables that form part of regional food systems. Some
are gathered seasonally, while others are grown around homes,
farms and village settlements.
Their names, nutritional composition and culinary uses vary between

1. Title and Regional Identity
sections.history:

A. Origin story
Leafy vegetables have long contributed to traditional diets. Communities
have selected, cultivated and gathered different plants according to their local
environments, food preferences and seasonal availability.
B. Cultural meaning
Indigenous greens reflect the connection between local biodiversity and
everyday cooking. They can contribute variety to meals and preserve knowledge of
plant identification, preparation and seasonal harvesting.
C. Story and folklore
Traditional knowledge may include the local names of plants, when
particular leaves are harvested, which parts are eaten and how they are prepared.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3. Main Ingredients and Preparation Method
A. The dough or base
For a leafy-green preparation, a separate dough is usually unnecessary.
The leaves form the principal ingredient.
B. The filling
Depending on the local dish, greens may be combined with coconut,
lentils, onions, garlic or spices. Some preparations use leafy greens as a filling for
flatbreads or dumplings.
C. The cooking technique
A general preparation method is:
1.Identify the edible species correctly.
2.Remove damaged leaves and unwanted material.
3.Wash the leaves thoroughly with clean water.

Moringa has a long history of cultivation and use in South Asian food

Moringa is closely associated with everyday home cooking. Drumstick

title: Ghavan
subtitle: Konkan rice pancake

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and regional details
Name of the food: Ghavan (Ghavane).
Region/community:
Konkan region of Maharashtra.
Common in Malvani and other Konkani-speaking households.
Also found in neighbouring coastal areas.
Context:
Ghavan is a thin, soft pancake made mainly from rice. It is traditionally
eaten for breakfast with coconut chutney, spicy curry, jaggery or homemade
butter. Rice is an important crop in the Konkan region, so this dish reflects the
local agricultural lifestyle.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Ghavan developed as part of the rice-based food traditions of the Konkan
coast. Its exact inventor and date of origin are not documented. Local rice
was soaked, ground and converted into batter for making fresh pancakes.
Origin story:
Cultural meaning:
Represents the rice-growing culture of coastal Maharashtra.
Commonly prepared as a household breakfast.
Reflects the use of simple local ingredients and traditional cooking skills.
Story / folklore:
In many coastal households, breakfast preparations such as ghavan were
part of everyday family life. The recipe was traditionally taught by mothers
and grandmothers. There is no widely documented specific folk legend about
its origin.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main ingredients and preparation method
The dough / batter:
Raw rice or rice flour
Water
Salt
The filling:
Ghavan normally has no filling. It is a plain rice pancake. Coconut chutney,
curry or jaggery may be served alongside it.
Cooking technique:
1.Wash and soak rice for several hours.
2.Grind it into a smooth batter.
3.Add water and salt to achieve a thin consistency.
4.Pour the batter onto a hot tawa.
5.Spread it into a thin pancake and cook until done.
6.Serve hot with chutney or curry.

title: Bajra Raab

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and regional details
Name of the food: Bajra Raab, also called Bajre ki Raab.
Region/community:
Rajasthan
Gujarat
Particularly associated with rural and farming communities.
Context:
Bajra Raab is a traditional porridge or drink made from pearl millet flour. It
is consumed warm and can be prepared in sweet or savoury versions. It was
useful in regions where pearl millet grows well in dry climatic conditions.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin story:
Bajra has been cultivated in dry parts of India for generations. Raab
developed as a practical preparation using locally available millet flour, water,
spices and sometimes buttermilk.
Cultural meaning:
Represents the millet-based food culture of Rajasthan and Gujarat.
Connected with farming households and rural food habits.
Shows how people adapted their diets to dry climates and local crops.
Story / folklore:
Raab was traditionally prepared in rural homes as a simple, filling food.
Farmers and families consumed it as part of their everyday diet. Its recipes
vary between households, and there is no single universally recorded origin
legend.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main ingredients and preparation method
The dough / base:
Bajra flour (pearl millet flour)
Water.
The filling:
There is no filling. Common additions include:
Jaggery for sweetness
Ginger powder
Ajwain
Cumin
Buttermilk in some regional versions
Cooking technique:
Heat ghee in a cooking pot.
Add ajwain or other spices.
Add bajra flour and roast gently.
Slowly add water while stirring to prevent lumps.
Add jaggery, salt or ginger according to the recipe.
Simmer until the mixture becomes smooth and thick.
Serve warm.
A recipe for Bajra Raab is also documented in the FSSAI's millet recipe material.

Traditional roasting and stirring require attention to prevent lumps and

replacing some traditional preparations.
Decline in traditional milling:
Traditionally, millet grains were cleaned and ground locally. The use of
packaged refined flour and reduced household grain processing can weaken
this knowledge.

title: Jowar Ambil
subtitle: Fermented sorghum drink

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and regional details
Name of the food: Jowar Ambil (Jwarichi Ambil).
Region/community:
Maharashtra, especially Vidarbha and Marathwada.
Traditionally associated with rural and farming households.
Context:
Jowar Ambil is a traditional sour porridge or drink prepared using
sorghum. Depending on the household, it may be made with jowar flour
or soaked and ground whole grain, then mixed with buttermilk. It is often
consumed during hot weather.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin story:
Jowar has long been an important crop in Maharashtra, particularly in
areas with lower rainfall. Ambil developed as a practical way of preparing
sorghum as a filling and refreshing food.
Cultural meaning:
Represents traditional millet-based diets.
Reflects the food habits of farming communities.
Shows the use of fermentation and souring in traditional
cooking.
Story / folklore:
In some rural households, ambil was prepared in the evening and left to
sour overnight. It was then consumed the next day, especially during hot
summer months. Family members passed the preparation method from
one generation to another.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main ingredients and preparation method
The dough / base:
Jowar flour or soaked whole jowar
Water
The filling:
There is no filling. The drink may include:
Buttermilk or curd
Salt
Green chillies
Ginger
Cumin
Cooking technique:
Mix jowar flour with water to make a smooth mixture.
Cook it while stirring until it forms a thin gruel.
Allow it to cool.
Mix in buttermilk or curd.
Leave it to sour for several hours or overnight, depending on the recipe.
Add salt and spices.
Serve cool.

title: Ker-Sangri

sections.regionalDetails:
1) Title and regional details
Name of the food: Ker-Sangri.
Region/community:
Rajasthan, especially the Thar Desert region.
Traditionally associated with Marwari households and desert communities.
Context:
Ker-Sangri is a traditional Rajasthani dish made from ker berries and sangri
pods. These ingredients come from plants that survive in dry desert
conditions. They are often dried and stored for later use.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin story:
Ker-Sangri developed from the need to use plants that grow naturally
in Rajasthan's dry environment. Fresh vegetables were not always easily
available, so desert berries and pods were collected, dried and
preserved.
Cultural meaning:
1.Represents Rajasthan's desert food heritage.
2.Shows the traditional use of native plants.
3.Commonly served at weddings and festive meals.
4.Reflects traditional food storage and preservation practices.
Story / folklore:
Ker-Sangri is connected with the resourcefulness of desert
households. People collected seasonal berries and pods, dried them in
the sun and stored them for future meals. It became a recognised part
of Rajasthani food culture. There is no single established folk legend
explaining its invention.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:
3) Main ingredients and preparation method
The dough / base:
There is no dough. The main ingredients are:
Ker – desert berries
Sangri – dried pods of the khejri tree
The filling:
There is no filling. Other ingredients include:
1.Mustard oil
2.Red chilli powder
3.Cumin
4.Coriander powder
5.Turmeric
6.Salt
7.Amchur or other souring ingredients, depending on the recipe
Cooking technique:
1.Soak dried ker and sangri in water.
2.Wash them thoroughly to remove
excess bitterness and impurities.
3.Boil or cook until tender.
4.Heat mustard oil in a pan.
5.Add cumin and spices.
6.Add the ker and sangri.
7.Cook until the ingredients absorb the
spices.
8.Serve with bajra roti or another
traditional bread

frequency of traditional desert dishes in some homes.
Decline in traditional milling:

culture in which it is served.

1) Title and regional details
Name of the food: Patholi, also known as Patoleo or Patoyo.
Region/community:
Goa and the Konkan coast.
Prepared in Goan Hindu and Catholic households.
Related preparations are also found in coastal Karnataka.
Context:
Patholi is a traditional sweet made using rice paste, coconut and jaggery. It
is wrapped in turmeric leaves and steamed. It is prepared during festivals and
special family occasions.
sections.history:
2) History and cultural importance
Origin story:
Patholi belongs to the old rice-based food traditions of the Konkan coast.
Its exact inventor and date of origin are not documented. Its ingredients reflect
the coastal availability of rice, coconut, jaggery and turmeric leaves.
Cultural meaning:
Prepared for Nag Panchami.
Made in Goa for the Feast of the Assumption on 15 August.
Also prepared during Ganesh Chaturthi and other family celebrations.
Represents the sharing of traditional food among family members and
neighbours.
Story / folklore:
In some Goan households, families gather during the monsoon season to
prepare Patholi. Different family members wash the turmeric leaves, spread the
rice batter, add the filling and fold the parcels. The aroma of turmeric leaves is
closely associated with festive memories.
sections.ingredientsAndPreparation:

The filling:
Fresh grated coconut
Jaggery
Cardamom or cinnamon (optional)

Soaked rice or rice flour
Water
A little salt

Cooking technique:
1.Wash and dry fresh turmeric leaves.
2.Spread rice paste over each leaf.
